ai-8ea62b1fb6.fulltext:
Anthropic shares closed about 17% higher on their first day of trading on Thursday, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety over the technology. The shares ended the session at around $97, up from a record-breaking IPO price of $83, after opening at $111.50 and briefly valuing the creator of the Claude chatbot at about $2tn – making the AI giant’s debut the biggest in history. The company’s valuation after the close stands at around $1.3tn, down from the high of $2tn recorded earlier.
However, a 2% slump at the close suggests that Anthropic’s stellar debut wasn’t enough to carry the wider market, which struggled for much of the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 2.2%, while the S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3%, preliminary data showed. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight day - its longest losing streak since 19 April 2024 – amid concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom and after the drama surrounding Nvidia following the fall of its CEO Jensen Huang last week dragged the company’s shares down.
Shortly before ringing the Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued a warning about the dangers of AI but said they weren’t inevitable. “We’ve always been honest that this techology has very real risks … from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems,” he said. “Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people making AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety.”

Anthropic’s listing will serve as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry – in particular, OpenAI, the parent company of ChatGPT – will be watching closely how it fares on the public market as time goes on.
Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.
Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:
This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.
Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this:No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.
The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.
Schiff goes on to remind the reader: “We have seen this movie before.” Invoking the bank bailout of 2008, he writes: “If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”
The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.
Anthropic has made a blockbuster stock market debut – shattering already high expectations.
The AP has put together some numbers to help you understand Thursday’s IPO:
The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: $81bn. That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday’s trading, it offered 980m shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75bn in June.

By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That’s still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75tn. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1tn. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95tn.
Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S+P 500: 11
Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1tn, followed by Microsoft ($3.8tn) and Nvidia ($3.6tn), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S+P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1tn. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018 .

Wall Street closes sharply lower as Anthropic's debut fails to revive AI enthusiasm
It’s just gone 4pm ET, which means trading in New York has closed for the day. US stocks slumped at the close, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalize faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early soar in its share price ebbed.
All three major US stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S+P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.
According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.
Anthropic’s record-setting IPO was priced late on Wednesday at $83 per share, and the stock opened at $111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed $2tn, its momentum began to lose steam.
Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others. And Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.
The Wall Street investment bankers that worked on Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering are set to be awarded a record $550m in underwriting fees, according to the official filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
That is more than they made on SpaceX, which set the previous record at $500m.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley will earn the biggest cut, taking over $200m between them.

The opening price of $111.50 per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to around $150bn at the current share price.
Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include the Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher and Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.
Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.
Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes which it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.
Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.
In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

world-3a99f6acf2.headline: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
world-3a99f6acf2.fulltext:
[Text below is Yahoo! Finance Canada's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
By Che Pan and Wen-Yee Lee
Nov 19 (Reuters) - Taiwan's TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The move could close one of the last remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful AI processors, complicating Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC.
The world's largest contract chipmaker has instructed that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said.
Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) or require advanced packaging, according to TSMC guidance reviewed by the two people.
Most leading AI chips are produced using 7-nanometre processes or smaller, enabling faster and more energy-efficient performance. HBM allows processors to handle the vast data volumes required by AI applications, while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.
US CLOSES MANUFACTURING ROUTE
The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday, removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licences.
Previously, TSMC could check the computing power and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls.
Under the new rules, TSMC can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.
The Financial Times first reported on Thursday that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.
CHINA'S AI CHIP AMBITIONS
The measures could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia's processors, including independent chip designers and technology giants that have developed in-house chips.
A US government list of approved chip designers includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek, but no mainland Chinese firms.
Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access to TSMC's 7-nanometre manufacturing technology before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said. Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

world-09f257575d.headline: Top UN court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Muslim Rohingya
world-09f257575d.fulltext:
[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
UN’s top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
ICJ ruling is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court.
In a landmark verdict, the United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population in a brutal 2017 military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The ruling at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court, and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
Evidence showed Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 Rohingya people, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” he said.
In the specific cases that he referred to, Iwasawa said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
‘Deeply emotional’
The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar welcomed the judgement but stressed that the decision must lead to concrete accountability measures and reparations for victims.
Founding member Yanghee Lee said in a statement that it was a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
“For decades, the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence, and dismiss our suffering,” said Wai Wai Nu, executive director of the Women’s Peace Network and a former political prisoner.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Gambia, which brought the case to the court, called the ruling “a historic day for international justice” and urged Myanmar to comply “fully and without delay”.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom would expel Myanmar’s defence attache and called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the judgement.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
‘Waiting’ years for justice
Reporting from the Hague, Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen said the verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya”.
“They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states, and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

Paytm shares plunged nearly 11 percent and Pine Labs fell about 5 percent, extending morning losses amid reports of a possible delay in implementing MDR on select UPI transactions and substantially lower charges on merchant-to-merchant payments.
  November 19, 2026 / 13:08 IST  
Shares of Paytm and Pine Labs extended their morning losses on Thursday, November 19, amid reports that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) on select Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions could face further delays, while charges on merchant-to-merchant transactions may be set substantially lower than initially feared.
Paytm parent One 97 Communications plunged 10.8 percent to Rs 1,686 in afternoon trade, emerging as the top midcap loser, after falling 6 percent earlier in the day. Pine Labs declined 4.9 percent to Rs 161, extending its morning loss of 3.8 percent. Both stocks substantially underperformed the broader market, with the Sensex and Nifty rising over 0.5 percent each.
The declines followed reports that the proposed MDR framework, which could provide an additional revenue stream for payment companies, may not be implemented until after the assembly elections scheduled in five states in the first half of 2027. According to a Financial Express report, the government remains wary of a potential backlash from merchants and trade associations over the introduction of transaction charges.
Although much of the regulatory and operational groundwork has been completed, the government, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) have yet to reach a consensus on the implementation timeline. The report cited an industry official as saying the rollout could even be deferred until after the Uttar Pradesh elections, although this was described as a worst-case scenario rather than the most likely outcome.
Adding to concerns over the potential revenue opportunity, the Business Standard reported that merchant-to-merchant (M2M) transactions on UPI are set to attract a flat fee of just Rs 5 under the proposed MDR framework, substantially lower than the charges of up to Rs 300 that traders had feared. The proposed flat fee would apply to transactions between wholesalers and retailers, business-to-business marketplaces and B2B collections.
According to the report, the decision was taken by NPCI's UPI and Services Steering Committee, although the implementation date remains undecided. The proposal comes amid opposition from merchant associations, with the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation seeking an exemption for M2M transactions from the MDR framework.
Meanwhile, the Payments Council of India has made multiple representations to the finance ministry and NPCI, seeking clarity on the implementation timeline, according to The Economic Times. The industry has also flagged that government incentive payments for processing UPI and RuPay debit-card transactions have remained outstanding for more than 18 months, even as technology, merchant acquisition and compliance costs continue to rise.
Payment companies have warned that prolonged uncertainty could affect investments in digital payment infrastructure, particularly in smaller towns and rural areas.
The proposed MDR framework could create additional revenue opportunities for payment companies, although the eventual benefit would depend on the charges, transaction categories covered and revenue-sharing arrangements.
Despite Thursday's steep decline, Paytm shares have gained 30.7 percent year-to-date, substantially outperforming the Nifty 50, which has fallen 3 percent over the same period. Meanwhile, Pine Labs has lost 31.5 percent this year. At the latest traded prices, Paytm's market capitalisation stood at approximately Rs 1.08 lakh crore, while Pine Labs was valued at Rs 18,590 crore.

world-9e020bee17.headline: Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
world-9e020bee17.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
world-9e020bee17.fulltext:
Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.
The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.
Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.
“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.
What was the pledge?
In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.
Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.
Data centres’ growing footprint
A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.
About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.
A wider retreat
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.
The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.
Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.
Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

india-deep-tech-ba91e15008.headline: Rs 50,000 cr arms export target may be met in 2028-29, multiple BrahMos talks on, says Defence Secretary
india-deep-tech-ba91e15008.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint

New Delhi: India could achieve the target of Rs 50,000 crore in annual defence exports by the 2028-29 financial year, a year before the 2029-30 deadline, Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh said Wednesday at an industry event. This would mean a roughly 30 percent jump from the Rs 38,424 crore of defence exports in 2025-26.
Defence exports have already reached Rs 23,479.34 crore in 2026-27 by the start of November, or about three-fifths of the Rs 38,424.01 crore achieved in 2025-26.
“We will achieve the Rs 50,000-crore defence exports target perhaps one year in advance,” said Singh, adding that it should be viewed as a “validation” of the country’s defence manufacturing industry and a reflection of its maturity. India is “exporting everything from artillery to bulletproof jackets”, he said.
Speaking as part of a panel at an event to mark the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) annual general meeting and annual convention that is to be convened Thursday, Singh underlined the overall goal: “[We] intend to grow Indian private [sector] national champions in this space.”
Responding to another question on exports of high-value platforms, including the Indo-Russian BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, Singh indicated that such exports would gain further traction in overseas markets. “There will be fairly significant exports of platforms as well,” he said. Singh pointed out, however, that artillery shells have been the “hero of export performance due to the ongoing conflict in Europe”. On the BrahMos specifically, Singh said many negotiations were ongoing, without specifying with whom.
Responding to a question on the budgetary allocation for defence in 2027-28, Singh said, “[The] focus is on higher capital expenditure, with the attendant multiplier effect on the economy.” Indicating that he had sought a higher percentage growth in the capital outlay component of the defence budget, he said, “We are confident of a 20 percent growth in capital expenditure [allocation] in compound annual growth rate terms, on top of the 22 percent [growth] last year.”
The defence services capital outlay for 2026-27 stands at Rs 2.19 trillion, nearly 22 percent more than the 2025-26 Budget Estimate (BE) of Rs 1.80 trillion. Within this, Rs 1.85 trillion is set aside for capital acquisition, or the modernisation capital budget, a rise of over 24 percent on the 2025-26 BE for the same head. This is the pot that pays for aircraft, ships, tanks, weapons, missiles and other military equipment.
Underscoring, however, that fund utilisation was more crucial than allocation, Singh said, “[In the] last two years, there was Rs 2 lakh crore plus of contract signings each year. This year, we have done Rs 80,000 crore [so far], with several big-ticket acquisitions on the anvil.” He expressed confidence that contract signings would hit another “record high” in 2026-27.
On the direction of ongoing defence sector reforms in 2027, Singh listed the outcomes he wanted to see, saying the country should have “at least 2-3 military aircraft manufacturers, multiple missile manufacturers, multiple ammo manufacturers”. This, he added, would establish the industrial surge capacity necessary to withstand a long conflict. “In new areas like drones, [we want] hundreds of companies.”
Surge capacity refers to the ability to rapidly expand military production, especially during a conflict.
“Whatever reforms are required, on the demand side in terms of visibility of orders and the supply side on ease of doing business or relaxed and faster licensing processes, all of those steps, the government will take,” said Singh.

indian-startups-cfab833427.headline: Physical AI startup Humyn Labs raises $47M in Series A
indian-startups-cfab833427.fulltext:
Physical AI startup Humyn Labs raises $47M in Series A
Humyn Labs said it will use the funds across three areas: building deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India; and expanding its R&D and market presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul.
Humyn Labs, a physical AI research and deployment startup, has raised $47 million in a Series A funding round comprising equity and debt.
The Bengaluru-headquartered startup raised $26 million in equity funding led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence (through Bajaj Finance), Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading LLC and angel investor Anita Pramoda, former CFO of Epic.
The $21 million venture debt round was led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
Founded in February 2026 by Manish Agarwal and Ishank Gupta, Humyn Labs prepares physical AI systems for real-world deployment by translating human experience into physical understanding for robots. The startup's proprietary capture devices record how people perform specific tasks across factories, warehouses, farms and homes. Its end-to-end data engine then converts these recordings into labelled, training-ready datasets with verified provenance across sight, sound, motion and touch.
Humyn Labs will use the funds across three areas: building deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India; and expanding its R&D and market presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul.
“Physical AI will only be as good as the real-world data it learns from. This funding will help us strengthen our research, build trust with labs and enterprises, and expand our global presence. With a $10 billion opportunity emerging in data infrastructure, we aim to build a $1 billion annual revenue business and establish ourselves as a global leader in the space,” said Manish Agarwal, Co-founder, Humyn Labs.
According to Humyn Labs, it has surpassed $50 million in annualised revenue within six months of operations. It works with frontier AI labs, robotics companies and world-model developers, and runs its own capture and enrichment operations across 20+ countries in Latin America, East Asia, and South and Southeast Asia.
“A robot does not learn a job from the internet. It learns it from the person who has done it for twenty years, on the floor where it will be done. We bring the model lab and the site operator onto that floor together, so every deployment teaches the next model, and the world’s factories, farms and warehouses become the training se,” said Ishank Gupta, Co-founder, Humyn Labs.

India’s carbon market is going live; its financial system can’t see it
Gaps in accounting, corporate disclosures and regulation could leave lenders and investors unable to assess the financial risks and opportunities the market creates
Visual Credits: Riddhi Tandon
India’s carbon market is about to involve real money. Carbon credit certificates (CCCs) under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme are expected to begin trading on the power exchanges shortly. Some 490 industrial units now carry binding emission-intensity targets, and draft targets for 255 steel plants are in the pipeline. Abroad, India has signed Article 6 agreements with Japan and South Korea, and carbon markets are again on the agenda at COP31, now under way in Antalya.
Carbon is becoming a balance-sheet item for Indian companies: a cost when they miss a target, an asset when they beat it and, for project developers, potentially an export. Yet India’s accounting, disclosure and data systems do not capture it consistently. A bank lending to a cement major, or a mutual fund holding a refinery, will find it hard to judge how exposed that company is based on public information.
The sums are not trivial, even at launch. Assuming a price of about USD 10 a tonne, Climate Risk Horizons estimated in July that buying credits to cover 2026-27 shortfalls would cost India’s five largest steelmakers about 7 per cent of their 2024-25 profits, and SAIL about 15 per cent. As targets tighten, as they must, companies that lag will face larger shortfalls, likely at higher prices. Inaction on decarbonisation will mean that exposure grows every time targets are tightened.
That exposure comes in two tiers. The first is a compliance cost: a company that misses its target must cover the shortfall by surrendering certificates, banked or bought at the market price. The second is a penalty: a company that fails to surrender enough pays environmental compensation at twice the average traded price. The first rises with the carbon price; the second arises only on non-compliance, which a lender should read as a warning sign.
Lenders meet this exposure at four points: reading a borrower’s accounts, monitoring its risk, labelling a loan green, or financing a carbon project. At each point, they hit a gap.
Accounting: India has no dedicated, comprehensive guidance on accounting for CCCs that companies earn, buy or bank, or for the obligation to surrender them. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India’s (ICAI) 2012 guidance covers only Kyoto-era Clean Development Mechanism credits. Companies can apply general accounting principles, but without specific guidance, similar positions may be recorded differently. Tax is also unclear: the 10 per cent rate on carbon-credit income in section 194 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 refers to UNFCCC-validated credits, which may exclude domestic CCCs. A lender comparing two cement borrowers cannot be sure it is comparing like with like.
Data: To place a borrower in the right tier, a lender needs four numbers: its target, its verified intensity, the certificates it holds and its expected shortfall. Only the target is routinely public. Plant emissions per tonne of product, company emissions per rupee of revenue and national emissions per unit of GDP serve different purposes. The problem is the missing bridge between them. SEBI’s BRSR Core asks listed companies for company-level emissions per rupee of revenue, adjusted for purchasing power parity, and per unit of output they define themselves. An investor cannot readily connect a company’s scheme target to its BRSR disclosure, its absolute emissions or its financial exposure. To make matters more confusing, the methodology behind the sectoral targets has not been made public.
Claims: Under offset rules issued by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), credits from activities outside the government’s Article 6 list may be sold abroad without a “corresponding adjustment” and continue to count towards India’s own target. That is legitimate in itself: such credits finance mitigation without the same tonne being counted against two national targets. The risk lies in what buyers claim with them, and the same applies at home. Indian companies buy voluntary credits to support net-zero claims, but BRSR Core does not ask them to disclose the volume, vintage, standard or adjustment status of those credits. Without that, ESG funds and green lenders cannot test the claims they rely on.
Bankability: CCCs have a statutory basis under the Energy Conservation Act, and Central Electricity Regulatory Commission’s (CERC) 2026 regulations govern their trading. The law does not yet settle whether certificates can be pledged, how that security is enforced, or how they are treated in insolvency. For Article 6, the government has not published a process, timeline or revocation rule for authorising credits. These gaps need not stop financing, but they raise its cost.
A new handbook for senior officials, from the Climate Vulnerable Forum’s V20 finance ministers and the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative (VCMI), asks host governments to estimate how much mitigation they can safely export. For India, that figure can be modelled from GDP and emissions projections and the NDC’s capacity and forest-sink targets, but none has been published. Financiers pricing Indian credits are left to make their own estimates.
None of this requires India to change its climate targets. It requires the financial system to catch up with the market the government has built. Five steps would help:
(i) The ICAI and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs should issue guidance on accounting for CCCs, surrender obligations and internationally transferred credits.
(ii) BEE and the scheme’s registry, Grid Controller of India, should publish plant-level verified emissions, issuances and surrenders annually
(iii) SEBI should add carbon credit use to BRSR Core and ask covered companies to reconcile their scheme performance with their reported emissions
(iv) The Finance Ministry should clarify the legal nature of CCCs, including their use as collateral, and their income tax and GST treatment
(v) The Reserve Bank of India, whose climate-risk disclosure rules for lenders were reportedly put on hold this year, should at least ask banks to factor rising compliance costs into credit assessments of covered borrowers.
At COP31, India will rightly defend its development space. At home, the more urgent task is less glamorous: making carbon visible on balance sheets. A market that finance cannot see is a market that cannot move finance.
Sagar Asapur is the Head of Sustainable Finance at Climate Risk Horizons. The views are the author’s own.

Chinese tech firms face a double hit as chip shipments stop and overseas cloud access disappears
The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.
Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. Chinese firms had been skirting US sanctions by renting compute capacity in third countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Those data centers now need a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that regulates sensitive technologies and enforces US export controls. Existing operators have a 90-day transition period and must rigorously screen their customers for ties to China.
According to the law firm Sidley Austin, the licensing requirement kicks in at an extremely low threshold equivalent to roughly 300 modern AI chips, while Chinese labs typically need several thousand processors. The Information reports that Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million contract with a Southeast Asian cloud provider in Indonesia in response and paused talks on additional deals.
Moonshot had planned to rent a large cluster of Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips there starting next year to train its next language model, Kimi K4. Because of the heavy compute demand, the company had agreed to prepay about 50 percent instead of the industry-standard 15 percent. Access to Blackwell chips abroad was already critical for its predecessor model K3, which matched top US models in July and triggered a BIS investigation, The Information also reported.
Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin are warning of rising training costs, and banks are pulling back too. According to Bloomberg, five lenders are considering dropping out of a $480 million loan for Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which was supposed to supply Nvidia chips in Malaysia for TikTok parent ByteDance.
TSMC and Samsung halt chip shipments to China
Beyond cloud restrictions, the new US rules are also starting to cut physical supply chains. The Financial Times reports that contract manufacturers TSMC and Samsung stopped certain processor shipments to Chinese customers in recent days while they apply for Commerce Department licenses. The move hits Chinese tech firms at a time when they are already struggling with historically high memory chip prices and capacity bottlenecks at domestic foundries such as SMIC. Huawei recently told its customers to source their own memory for its new AI chip.
The new BIS rules block a workaround through independent packaging and testing firms that Chinese chip designers had used to order high-performance processors without getting direct US approval. Samsung's affected customers include ByteDance and Baidu's AI data center unit Kunlun. Exemptions for non-AI chips have also been eliminated, so TSMC and Samsung now need licenses even for advanced smartphone processors from manufacturers including Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo. Industry insiders say that is likely to cause significant production delays.
Alibaba's covert network reached China's military research
A New York Times investigation into the background of the espionage scandal involving Jensen Huang's former mistress Alice Huang shows why Washington tightened controls so aggressively. According to the Times, Alibaba acted as the secret primary customer and financier behind Alice Huang's Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which bought more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Nvidia's sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang in 2022.
Through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, Megaspeed operated cutting-edge Nvidia chips on behalf of Alibaba in a data center in Johor built by Malaysian conglomerate YTL, in an analysis by security firm Infrawatch that is said to show this. Megaspeed reportedly sourced the servers from Aivres, a US subsidiary of state-linked Chinese firm Inspur, had them maintained by technicians from Shanghai, and routed data to China through fiber-optic and undersea cables via Singapore. Some chips were reportedly also smuggled physically.
A contingency contract gives Alibaba direct access to all servers, chips, and intellectual property if Megaspeed breaches their agreement. YTL's stock price fell 20 percent amid the investigations.
Alibaba also has a direct connection to Zhejiang Lab in Hangzhou, co-founded in 2017, which links civilian and military research. The lab is run by former Alibaba CTO Wang Jian, a longtime friend of Jensen Huang who also advises the People's Liberation Army's National Defense University, an institution on the US sanctions list.
Researchers at the lab use Nvidia hardware to work on, among other things, AI-driven cyberattacks and automated vulnerability discovery, according to the New York Times. They also work with a Chinese air force academy on war-game simulations against foreign carrier strike groups. Through the state-owned firm Zhejiang Computility and suppliers tied to the business network of Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, Alibaba built data centers with export-controlled Nvidia processors for the lab, even though the company officially denies any military use of its services.

ai-2ad2190c7a.headline: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity
ai-2ad2190c7a.fulltext:
Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees.
As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.
First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.
The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.
Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.
Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.
Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.
All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.
Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.
Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

indian-startups-300c7c7883.headline: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
indian-startups-300c7c7883.fulltext:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.
That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.
Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day.
Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.
Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.
Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.
Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “early talks” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.
There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.
Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?
When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.
How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?
I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.
How far behind are open models right now?
A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.
If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?
Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.
In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?
We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.
Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.
On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.
Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?
Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.
Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?
I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.
How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?
Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?
It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

india-deep-tech-ad8e88fef3.source: Defence BREAKING NEWS | Defence LATEST NEWS | Defence NEWS TODAY | Defence LIVE UPDATES | Defence TRENDING NEWS | – ThePrint
india-deep-tech-ad8e88fef3.fulltext:
New Delhi: The Indian Air Force (IAF) expects to receive its first squadron of the crucial indigenous Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) jets, whose deliveries have been delayed, by the end of March 2027 at the latest, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said on Monday.
“Very shortly, we will have LCA [Tejas] Mk1A joining [the] Indian Air Force. Within this financial year, we will have a squadron. Then we will continue developing; we will take it further… LCA [Tejas] Mark-2 will roll out maybe next year. And we are working very hard also for AMCA (Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft),” said the Air Chief Marshal in response to a question at a media summit in New Delhi.
An IAF squadron typically comprises 18 aircraft, and the force has ordered a total of 180 Tejas Mk1A jets. The IAF is currently at its lowest strength in 60 years, with 29 active fighter squadrons against a sanctioned strength of 42.
ThePrint was the first to report last week that the first one or two Tejas Mk1A jets are likely to be handed over to the IAF early in 2027, possibly as soon as January.
#WATCH | ANI National Security Summit 3.0 | Delhi: On when can we see the Tejas Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Mark-1A (Mk1A) fighter jets getting inducted, Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit says, "Creating indigenous capability in fully designed, developed,… pic.twitter.com/azZg5aA4CC
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
Also Read: R&AW is being blamed in Bangladesh for air force pilot’s death. It’s a red herring
Why have deliveries been delayed?
State-run aerospace and defence company Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) missed its original February 2024 deadline to begin deliveries of the first batch of 83 Mk1A jets, contracted in February 2021 for Rs 36,400 crore. The delay was primarily attributed to the late delivery of F404-IN20 engines by US manufacturer GE Aerospace.
The project was also affected by the complex process of integrating weapons and other systems. Deliveries of this first tranche were originally scheduled to be completed by February 2028.
In September 2025, HAL received a second order for 97 Mk1A aircraft, worth over Rs 62,370 crore. Deliveries under this contract are expected to begin in financial year 2027-28 and be completed over six years.
The Mk1A is an upgraded version of the indigenous Tejas Mk1 which is already operational with the IAF. Classified as a 4.5-generation fighter, it is equipped with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, which lets it scan faster, track several targets at once, detect adversaries from longer distances and resist jamming better.
The aircraft is also equipped with beyond-visual-range (BVR) missiles, allowing pilots to engage enemy aircraft from greater distances. Its electronic warfare suite protects it against adversary sensors and weapons.
The Tejas Mk2 is envisaged as a more advanced and heavier variant, powered by more powerful GE engines. However, its prototype has yet to take its first flight.
The AMCA, meanwhile, is India’s stealth combat aircraft under development. It is being pursued through an industry partnership model, and the process of selecting the company or consortium that will help develop and build its prototypes is underway.

deep-tech-75fbcd69cc.headline: Koduri’s Oxmiq Offers IP, Tools for Indian Teams to Design AI Chips
deep-tech-75fbcd69cc.fulltext:
In an exclusive interview, Raja Koduri, founder and CEO of Oxmiq Labs, discussed the company’s India initiative, the role of memory hierarchy in AI computing systems, custom silicon economics, and India’s infrastructure requirements.
Oxmiq Labs has developed tools and intellectual property (IP) to help teams in India design their own AI chips. The company is also working on an India initiative that it expects to detail in December, Koduri told EE Times.
“We have built tools to enable teams in India to make their own chips,” he said. “We are working on an initiative in India, and hopefully, when I return to India in December, I will be able to share some of those initiatives publicly.”
The aim, Koduri said, is to develop state-of-the-art chips designed to produce AI tokens as efficiently as possible.
Separately, Oxmiq is an architecture and engineering partner to AM Intelligence Labs, the AI compute division of AM Group, the parent company of Greenko, India’s renewable energy producer with a portfolio target of 50 GW by 2030. The partnership covers site selection, compute design, and partner selection. The initial build will use Nvidia GPUs, with locally developed designs to follow.
“To begin with, we are bringing the best technology available today, which is Nvidia GPUs,” he said. “But as we move toward 2030, we will also leverage designs developed in India.”
Koduri said India must develop its own designs, chips, and infrastructure to bring down the cost of converting electricity into AI output, even if manufacturing remains overseas.
“Chips designed in India can be manufactured in Taiwan or South Korea,” he said. “That is perfectly fine. But the products should be owned by India.”
Koduri said the main constraint in AI computing is how efficiently a data center converts power into AI output. At the technical level, he said, the memory hierarchy matters more than floating-point operations and compute.
“It is all a memory hierarchy problem, from NAND flash storage to double data rate [DDR] memory attached to the central processing unit [CPU], high-bandwidth memory [HBM] attached to the GPU, and static random-access memory [SRAM],” he said.
A startup might focus on one type of memory, such as SRAM, and position it as the answer to a particular computing problem. But Koduri said the system-level requirements are broader.
“We look at the problem as a memory hierarchy and exploit each level as efficiently as possible,” he said.
Asked what changes when energy, compute, cooling, networking, and software are designed together, Koduri said the industry has traditionally operated in separate layers. Chipmakers typically design and sell a chip to a systems company, which builds a system. Another company builds the rack, while a data center operator handles installation, thermal management, and cooling.
“There are multiple layers in the ecosystem before everything comes together,” he said.
However, the scale of AI data center expansion is changing how companies approach the design process. Koduri said engineers must consider the entire data center rather than optimize an individual chip in isolation.
“We have to think about the whole system,” he said. “Not just the system, but the entire data center.”
The objective, he explained, is to convert incoming electricity into tokens as efficiently as possible while managing the heat generated by the chips.
Koduri described this as an optimization problem that will continue to evolve as AI models and computing architectures change. Over the past five years, he said, the industry has moved from basic transformers to mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek optimizations, and decision-making models. GPU optimization is also continuing.
“The real constraint is that we have megawatts coming in and intelligence coming out,” he said. “How efficiently can we transform those megawatts into intelligence?”
Customers, Koduri said, care about the output of the complete system. “They want to plug in electricity, provide cooling, and get tokens they can sell. That is all.”
Oxmiq’s work with AM Intelligence Labs covers data center planning and the selection of technology partners, Koduri said.
The company’s support begins with site selection and data center design. It then works on compute design, rack placement, networking and storage requirements, thermal management, cooling, and software stack operations.
“We do not necessarily solve every problem ourselves,” Koduri said. “For example, we may select a suitable partner to provide the system, such as an original equipment manufacturer. That is the kind of support we are currently providing to [AM Group], because we come from the technology world, while they come from the energy world.”
Koduri pointed to AM Intelligence Lab’s first AI factory in Hyderabad, which he described as probably the first such deployment in Asia. The company has ordered about 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs for the 30-MW facility, with delivery of Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale systems scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. It has since placed an additional order for 20,000 Rubin GPUs for sites in India and Malaysia.
Koduri said companies can potentially improve computing efficiency by designing the silicon, systems, and infrastructure for a specific data center rather than relying entirely on components designed for a wide range of customers.
Traditionally, a chipmaker had to sell its product to many data centers to generate revenue. That required designing a flexible product that could accommodate different customer requirements, standards, and features, even if those compromises reduced efficiency.
“If I am designing for one data center and its specific constraints, I can build something that is twice as cost-effective,” he said.
For a 1-GW data center, which Koduri estimated could cost around $55 billion to build, he said custom-designing the system could potentially deliver twice the compute by using power more efficiently.
He said this approach could change both the engineering mindset and the business model. A company developing silicon could now target the data center problem itself, with a single customer potentially generating multibillion-dollar revenue.
Koduri said custom silicon, systems, and software begin to make economic sense for customers planning at least 100 megawatts (MW) of computing capacity.
He put the cost of 100 MW of computing capacity at approximately $5.5 billion using off-the-shelf hardware. By comparison, R&D for a state-of-the-art chip manufactured by TSMC could cost around $100 million to $150 million. Developing a complete custom system could cost up to about $500 million, even with generous spending, he said.
If a custom system roughly halved that cost, a customer could save more than $2 billion even after spending $500 million on development, he said.
However, customers need the IP, tools, and technical know-how to develop custom systems, and Koduri said Oxmiq is building a solution to that problem.
Koduri said Oxmiq’s customers fall into three categories. The first comprises infrastructure companies such as AM Intelligence Labs, which are building computing capacity and need support across the system. The second includes companies designing silicon for applications such as data centers, physical AI, and enterprise AI.
Oxmiq can provide hardware and software IP to startups developing products such as chips for robots, allowing them to focus on their customers’ requirements, Koduri said.
The third category includes companies developing new materials and new physics, such as new forms of memory, silicon, silicon photonics, and photonics-based interconnects. They can license Oxmiq’s IP rather than develop the computing technology alongside their research.
In India, Oxmiq is engaging with customers in the infrastructure and silicon design categories. In the U.S., it works across all three categories, with most customers in infrastructure and new-physics applications, he said.
India’s installed data center power capacity stood at 1.57 GW in August 2026, up from about 375 MW in 2020, and is projected to reach nearly 8 GW by 2030, according to the Indian Press Information Bureau. About $70 billion of investment is underway, with a further $90 billion in announced projects.
Koduri said a 1-GW data center costs approximately $55 billion to build. By comparison, he said capital expenditure per gigawatt in China was moving toward $10 billion. “They can get things done at one-fifth, and perhaps one-tenth, of the cost of the rest of the world,” he said.
He estimated that India would need at least 6 GW of infrastructure to provide intelligence to its entire population, adding that the actual requirement would be much higher. The combined GPU capacity currently available in India, including planned deployments by AM Intelligence Labs, would not reach 100 MW, he said. That suggests India would need to increase that capacity at least 60-fold before the end of the decade.
For Koduri, the opportunity is not limited to building more data centers. It also includes developing the chips, systems, and software that convert electricity into AI output. “The opportunities for design teams, systems teams, and software teams in India are tremendous,” he said. “This is a build-out that India should participate in.”

Alibaba Group Holding is accelerating its pivot to domestic microchips, as chief executive Eddie Wu Yongming said the company was training its next-generation AI models on in-house chips after reporting a better-than-expected uptick in revenue and profit.
“Infrastructure powered by our own domestically developed chips is becoming the foundation of Alibaba’s full-stack AI capabilities,” Wu said on Thursday during an earnings call, adding that the company’s proprietary chip development was progressing ahead of original expectations.
The CEO added that he expected the vast majority of artificial intelligence models developed by Alibaba, its partners and customers to rely entirely on domestic chips for both pre-training and post-training in the future.
The Chinese tech giant’s cloud revenue would grow by 50 per cent or more from 2028 as mass production of computing products scaled up, Wu said, though growth would likely stay at 30 to 45 per cent next year due to uncertainties related to the United States’ latest export restrictions.
Wu reaffirmed Alibaba’s target of hitting US$100 billion in external cloud revenue by 2030.
The company said on Thursday that during the quarter ended September 30, external recurring revenue tied to AI cloud and computing surged 67 per cent, lifting total revenue 10 per cent to a better-than-expected 271.5 billion yuan (US$40.5 billion).
The tech and e-commerce giant’s AI Cloud and Compute Services segment – comprising its cloud computing business and chip design unit T-Head, which filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong in September – rose 53 per cent to a revenue of 61 billion yuan, marking the fastest growth since late 2020.
Its AI-related product revenue delivered triple-digit growth for the thirteenth consecutive quarter, according to an earnings statement.
The firm’s 271.5 billion yuan total revenue for the quarter surpassed a Bloomberg consensus estimate of 270.5 billion yuan. Net income rose 213 per cent to 64.4 billion yuan, beating the 24.3 billion yuan projection.
Adjusted Ebita (earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation) – a key measure of operating profitability – grew 260 per cent to 32.6 billion yuan year on year.
Toby Xu, the chief financial officer, said: “As AI monetisation continues to ramp up, we will maintain disciplined investments in AI capabilities with a focus on return on invested capital while targeting to achieve positive free cash flow.”
Alibaba’s capital expenditure (capex), mainly to support its AI infrastructure buildout, reached 50.5 billion yuan during the period, down from 67.7 billion last quarter.
Meanwhile, free cash flow – a measure of operating cash flow minus capex – had an outflow of 34.5 billion yuan, compared with an outflow of 44.7 billion yuan in the June quarter. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
The latest results come as the US moves to tighten export controls over advanced chips, which could make it more difficult for Chinese tech companies to access cutting-edge US semiconductors and hamper the development of artificial intelligence models including Alibaba’s flagship Qwen family.
Wu added in the earnings call that evolving global compute policies might also prompt a downward revision of Alibaba’s 20-gigawatt data centre target.
Other major Chinese tech companies, meanwhile, reported quarterly revenue declines on Thursday.
Short-video platform Kuaishou reported an 11.1 per cent decline in revenue to 31.6 billion yuan and a net loss of 959 million yuan. Research and development spending rose 41.9 per cent, mainly on increased investment in its Kling AI video-generation business.
Video gaming giant NetEase’s revenue fell 1.8 per cent to 27.9 billion yuan, with games and related services revenue down 1.7 per cent. Net profit attributable to shareholders slipped 2.5 per cent to 8.4 billion yuan.
Alibaba’s AI Labs and Applications segment – covering AI model labs, the Qwen Consumer Business Group and workplace AI agent platform QwenWork – generated 4.4 billion yuan in revenue, a 51 per cent year-on-year increase.
Earlier this week, the company launched Qwen4-Max, its most advanced AI model, which it said was better than earlier models at addressing AI-enabled cyberattacks and offered superior reasoning capabilities while bringing down inference costs.
Alibaba’s core e-commerce business, the other key pillar of the 27-year-old company, reported a 2 per cent rise in revenue to 197.2 billion yuan, as the company navigates a cautious domestic consumer market.

India Hydrogen Alliance proposes INR 1,400-crore CfD funding pool to boost industrial green hydrogen offtake
The India Hydrogen Alliance (IH2A) has proposed a budgetary allocation of INR 1,400 crore ($150 million) to the Government of India to establish a Contract for Difference (CfD) funding framework and also submitted a five-point agenda to accelerate green hydrogen project development and boost industrial offtake in the country.
The proposals were submitted formally to the government.
IH2A, in its submission to the Government of India, asked for a review of the National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM) to address the slow pace of domestic industrial offtake and project development. It asked for demand side incentives for industrial users in refineries, steel, fertilizers and chemical sectors.
IH2A’s five-point agenda to improve green hydrogen project development and domestic offtake includes:
- Review of National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM). According to IH2A, the lack of demand side incentives is adversely affecting the pace of project development. It recommends sectoral mandates for industrial decarbonization with minimum green hydrogen offtake commitments increasing from 5-10% over the next five years in hard-to-abate sectors. IH2A recommends 10% green hydrogen purchase obligation or consumption mandates in large refineries, fertilizers, steel and chemical units by 2030. Other recommendations include Increasing support for industrial green hydrogen hubs with anchor industrial offtake units; aggregated public procurement for green and low-carbon hydrogen by refineries, the largest offtake sector for green hydrogen, to address procurement delays by refineries and its adverse impact on India’s national hydrogen transition ambitions and 2030 targets; and incentives for early adopters to build on operating experience from green hydrogen plants at Vijayanagar (Karnataka); Vijaypur, Guna (MP); and Bina (MP), and expand their capacity.
- Creation of a INR 1,400-crore Contract for Difference (CfD) funding pool and framework. Provide green hydrogen offtake support of $1.5/kg for 100,000 metric tonnes of green hydrogen procured by early adopters and industrial offtake units. ThisJapan-style CfD framework will incentivize domestic industrial plants to commit offtake from operational industrial green hydrogen plants in India. According to IH2A, this would enable new 750 MW electrolyser CAPEX to be deployed in domestic industrial projects and support industrial decarbonization in India.
- Creation of a national low carbon hydrogen standard. This standard,in addition to the existing National Green Hydrogen Standard, will provide flexibility to domestic industries to pursue decarbonization pathways.
- Government green steel mandates in automotive, construction, infrastructure and manufacturing sectors to support low carbon industrial use. Notify minimum thresholds for public procurement of green steel by PSUs and public contracts as it would support additional derived demand for green products and industrial use.
- A national green and low-carbon hydrogen skilling programme. Developing skills across production, storage, infrastructure and sector-specific industrial use will help to build Atmanirbharta (self-reliance) on industrial hydrogen gas production and use, leading to more jobs and skills in the clean hydrogen economy.
“The lack of demand side incentives or mandates has been a key reason for slow in project development. Without demand side support and green hydrogen offtake agreements, projects are unable to achieve Final Investment Decision (FID) closure and start placing equipment orders,” said Amrit Singh Deo, IH2A Secretariat lead. “India should replicate the Japan Contract for Difference (CfD) framework and create a INR 1400 crore CfD investment pool for early adopters and industrial offtake.”
