South Korea becomes fourth country globally to hit US$1 trillion exports on AI chip boom
This surpassed last year's record of US$709 billion, the country's trade ministry said.
SEOUL: South Korea's exports so far for this year have exceeded US$1 trillion, driven by a global AI chip boom, making it the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China.
Exports passed the US$1 trillion mark on Thursday (Nov 19), compared with last year's record of US$709 billion, the trade ministry said.
The export surge has been led by the semiconductor sector as AI investment drives demand, while other traditional manufacturing sectors, such as autos, steel and ships, have lagged amid global protectionism triggered by US tariffs and geopolitical conflicts such as the Iran war.
In the first three quarters of 2026, semiconductor exports jumped 184 per cent from a year earlier to account for 42 per cent of the country's total exports, more than double their average 20 per cent share over the past five years.
"Now, we need to turn this achievement into sustainable growth. We will enhance the competitiveness of major industries and grow future growth engines, such as AI and bio," President Lee Jae Myung said in a social media post on X.
"Most of all, the achievement in exports should improve the lives of the people. We will create 'growth for all', sharing the opportunities and fruits of growth with big and small companies as well as the capital area and regional areas," Lee said.
Despite record exports, domestic demand in Asia's fourth-largest economy remains weak, with the benefits of the export boom yet to trickle down to many households. Consumer sentiment has been hurt by high interest rates and prices, as well as unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market.
As part of efforts to tackle widening inequality in a two-speed economy, the Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won (US$121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to funnel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education.
"The government and the private sector will have to work together to strengthen the cycle of exports leading to domestic investment and job creation, as well as the revitalisation of regional economies, so that all people share the benefits of export growth in their daily lives," the country's six major business groups said in a joint statement, welcoming the US$1 trillion milestone.
Economic growth in South Korea, home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, is expected to accelerate to the mid-3 per cent range this year, after expanding 1 per cent last year, as the AI boom fuels exports and investments, the finance minister said last month.

global-economics-b0ecc5a639.headline: AI surge could strain US capacity and overheat economy, Fed's Goolsbee says
global-economics-b0ecc5a639.fulltext:
[Text below is CNA's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
AI surge could strain US capacity and overheat economy, Fed's Goolsbee says
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 : The booming rollout of artificial intelligence technology could strain the US economy's capacity and further boost inflation that the Federal Reserve will have to counteract, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said on Thursday, as AI firm Anthropic set a new record for an initial public offering of stock.
"The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy. I find it hard to ... look at that any other way," Goolsbee said in a conference call with reporters. "When you're getting major business investment, almost unprecedented levels of business investment, there's a high danger that the economy's capacity cannot handle that kind of a pig through the python."
Goolsbee said he sees the multitrillion-dollar pipeline of data-center projects already adding to what he referred to as "borderline, disturbingly high inflation rates" that are well above the Fed's 2 per cent target and potentially heading higher.
He said he felt the Anthropic IPO, giving the company's early shareholders the ability to tap equity holdings well in excess of $1 trillion, could on its own become relevant to the path of the broader economy.
"A $1.5 trillion IPO. The question of what people are going to do with the money now that they have some access to that liquidity is going to become a macro-relevant statistic," Goolsbee said. "We're watching that."
DATA-CENTER BACKLASH
The US central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point at its December 8-9 meeting. Fed policymakers also are wrestling with how the AI boom is influencing the economy.
The recent US midterm elections saw AI skepticism emerge at the polls, with municipalities in a number of states approving ballot initiatives that could limit how quickly and where data centers get built, potentially slowing the industry's breakneck evolution.
At the same time, the Fed this week held a high-level conference looking at the possible impact on productivity and the labor market should the new technologies diffuse through the economy and reach a potential that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has characterized as pivotal to US economic leadership.
In remarks at an earlier event on Thursday, Goolsbee said it was not yet clear what effect AI will have on productivity or the economy's underlying potential, noting that it took years — even decades — for other general-purpose technologies to change how businesses operated on a broad basis.
In the meantime, the Fed will have to cope with short-term effects that so far seem to be inflationary.
"The Fed's job is to prevent this thing from overheating the economy," with monetary policy set tight enough to keep demand and supply in balance, Goolsbee said at the event.
The Chicago Fed chief did not say if he would support a larger half-percentage-point rate hike at the December meeting, as at least one of his colleagues has advocated, but added that all options were on the table.
"The question of how steep the rate path is going to be and if there will be any rate increases should be determined, in my view, by whether you think inflation is going to be heading back to 2 per cent on its own or not," Goolsbee said. "The evidence does not suggest we're on a path back to 2 per cent."

US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
The US House Foreign Committee released the chip export licensing data amid Nvidia’s ex-CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
The Department of Commerce’s approvals covered exports of 879,000 chips, including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, the committee said on Thursday.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which fuelled renewed calls for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.
All four of the Chinese companies highlighted in the committee report are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
The committee chair, Brian Mast, has “exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD’s AI chip licenses for the People’s Republic of China”, the committee said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.
“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”. It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.
But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Nvidia’s stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent and the broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 were down 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

Karnataka hosts 1,088 of India’s 2,117 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), accounting for 51% of the national total, according to a report released on Thursday at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, 2026.
The report, titled ‘GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI’, prepared by Zinnov in collaboration with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission, outlines the concentration of enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities in the State compared to the rest of India.
As per the study, Karnataka houses 320 of India’s 506 Global 2000 GCCs (63%). Between FY 2021 and FY 2026, the State attracted 43% of all new GCCs entering India (217 of 510) and 54% of new centres established by U.S. West Coast-headquartered firms.
In terms of workforce, the State’s GCCs employ more than 829,000 people, representing 35% of the country’s installed GCC talent. The State also houses 1,11,000 AI and machine learning (ML) professionals, 43% of India’s GCC AI/ML workforce, and 60,000 of the nation’s 110,000 technical engineering leaders (55%).
Hiring data
Hiring data from 2024 to 2026 shows that Bengaluru accounted for 44% of senior AI-leadership GCC job postings in India and up to 63% of Distinguished or Principal AI Engineer roles.
The report also highlighted higher AI adoption rates among Karnataka-based centres compared to the national average. Surveyed GCCs in the State scored 1.12 times the national average on overall AI maturity, with 66% operating at the advanced ‘Portfolio Hub’ stage, compared to 43% nationally.
Across specific metrics, 69% of surveyed centres in Karnataka have dedicated AI budgets (versus 57% nationally), 83% reuse in-house AI platforms across business units (versus 57%), and 66% follow responsible AI practices (versus 49%).
Start-up density
Over 660 GCCs in Karnataka possess AI/ML capabilities, supported by more than 120 dedicated AI/ML Centres of Excellence, nearly half of India’s total of over 250, according to the study. Roughly one-third of these centres focus on generative or agentic AI. Additionally, Karnataka hosts over 29% of India’s AI start-ups, 15.4% of its incubators and accelerators, and produces over 1,30,000 STEM graduates annually.
To sustain this trajectory through 2030, the report outlines five priorities: expanding advanced GCC mandates, shifting towards global AI ownership, developing leadership, scaling measurable value and moving research into enterprise adoption.
State initiatives such as the IT Policy 2025-30, the ₹300 crore Nipuna Karnataka skilling programme and Beyond Bengaluru clusters aim to support these goals, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, Electronics, IT&BT, Government of Karnataka, while unveiling the report.

other-interests-2b675cf3be.headline: AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits
other-interests-2b675cf3be.fulltext:
Hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era. But they might soon be gone for good. Researchers have found that the latest large language models (LLMs) rarely, if ever, attribute information to sources that don’t exist.
The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple maths problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release new or updated models with improved capabilities. Many of these tendencies disappear about 16 months after the phenomenon is first described in a published paper. The analysis, described in a blog post, has not been peer reviewed.
“We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.
But just because an LLM behaviour fades as models improve doesn’t mean that the effect immediately disappears, says Maxim Topaz, a health-care AI researcher at Columbia University in New York City. Topaz has found1 that the number of hallucinated citations in academic papers has risen drastically since 2023, probably because more researchers than ever before are using LLMs, and they often aren’t using the latest models.
Trait lifespans
Queen and his colleague identified 50 widely cited LLM behaviours that were described in publications between late 2022, when some of the first LLMs became widely available, and late 2025. They then gave the same prompts that first elicited the behaviour in the original publications to 20 LLMs that were released from mid-2024 to late 2026 to see if the effect has strengthened or weakened over time. For example, they asked each model to count the number of r’s in ‘strawberry’ — something that LLMs have found difficult but can now do more reliably.
Nearly half of the behaviours they checked have largely disappeared from newer models, leading the researchers to deem those effects ‘expired’. Expired behaviours had an average lifespan of about 16 months after publication, although some were fleeting — models stopped overthinking simple maths problems just a month and a half after this tendency was published. Other traits persisted, such as the stereotyping of Black women by disproportionately describing them as resilient, which lasted for longer than three years.
Although most of the retested LLM behaviours have faded over time, three have become more pronounced. Today’s models praise what their users like even more often than they used to, LLMs more strongly favour their own writing compared with that of other LLMs and people; and LLMs are now even worse than they used to be at generating truly random numbers.

other-interests-94bd74060a.headline: Big tech may finally face legal consequences for AI’s actions
other-interests-94bd74060a.fulltext:
Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality.
Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers.
In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”.
Advertisement
Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive.
OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide.
What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash.
In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to.
I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “AI as Normal Technology” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident.
The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “impossible” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms.
Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies.
In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.”
Further AI reading
- After much fanfare, Anthropic has listed on the stock market at $83 a share, giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June.
- The Economist has a great piece on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive. It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food?
- The Cambridge Dictionary has named “human” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view.
- As the COP31 climate summit continues, only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI. As I have written previously, we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply.

It was the lithium that gave it away, says Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.
Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.
The lithium showed they were too late.
The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.
“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.
The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.
Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.
The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.
Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.
Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.
At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”
Design for demise
From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.
Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.
RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies
“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”
But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.
As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.
“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”
SpaceX launched its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.
Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.
Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.
“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”
Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he says, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”
There are reasons to be concerned.
Aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.
Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering plans. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.
“The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”
Conflicting models
One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”
Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.
But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”
To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are currently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”
To do better, scientists are developing new models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.
But state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.
To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”
That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.
Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens says.
But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

world-11685b3b01.headline: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
world-11685b3b01.fulltext:
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
- Published
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.
He added that, while ruling against Myanmar did not mean the court would find similarly with Gaza, if it had not found Myanmar responsible, the case against Israel "would, in effect, be over". Israel says the case against it is "wholly unfounded".
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, told the BBC that the court had not accepted Myanmar's counter-terrorism defence and had found for the first time that rape and sexual violence was an act of genocide, positions it would bear in mind for future cases.
A spokesperson for the US State Department said "the proper interpretation" of the Genocide Convention is of "paramount importance", and so is "preventing politicisation" of the International Criminal Court. "We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," they said.
They said they share the "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups", and added the US is the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response".
Following Thursday's ruling, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the government was ordering Myanmar's defence attaché be expelled and that he was summoning its charge d'affaires.
He pledged to set out "further action in the coming days to ensure those responsible are held to account" after a cross-party group of MPs called for the government to resume sanctions against Myanmar's military.

world-265f7253b1.headline: Reactions as top UN court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
world-265f7253b1.fulltext:
[Text below is Al Jazeera's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
UN’s top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
ICJ ruling is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court.
In a landmark verdict, the United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population in a brutal 2017 military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The ruling at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court, and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
Evidence showed Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 Rohingya people, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” he said.
In the specific cases that he referred to, Iwasawa said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
‘Deeply emotional’
The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar welcomed the judgement but stressed that the decision must lead to concrete accountability measures and reparations for victims.
Founding member Yanghee Lee said in a statement that it was a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
“For decades, the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence, and dismiss our suffering,” said Wai Wai Nu, executive director of the Women’s Peace Network and a former political prisoner.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Gambia, which brought the case to the court, called the ruling “a historic day for international justice” and urged Myanmar to comply “fully and without delay”.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom would expel Myanmar’s defence attache and called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the judgement.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
‘Waiting’ years for justice
Reporting from the Hague, Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen said the verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya”.
“They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states, and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

world-d6d5a75fc7.headline: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules
world-d6d5a75fc7.fulltext:
Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.
The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.
One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”
Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.
In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.
After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.
The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.
The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.
Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.
“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.
It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.
The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.

indian-startups-226b7f97e5.headline: AI startup Humyn Labs raises $47 million in Series A funding round
indian-startups-226b7f97e5.fulltext:
AI startup Humyn Labs raises $47 million in Series A funding round
Humyn Labs raises $47 million to expand global operations and build real-world robot testing infrastructure
Listen to This Article
Humyn Labs, a physical artificial intelligence (AI) research and deployment startup, raised $47 million in a Series A funding round to expand its global operations and build infrastructure for testing and deploying robots in real-world environments, the firm said on Wednesday.
The round comprises $26 million in equity, led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, angel investor Anita Pramoda, and Jump Trading LLC. The remaining $21 million was raised through venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.
In April this year, Humyn Labs announced a $20 million commitment to develop human data infrastructure for physical AI firms worldwide.  
In an interaction with Business Standard, its Cofounder Manish Agarwal said the startup plans to deploy fresh capital towards building deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea and India, expanding the company’s data-capture hardware and enrichment capabilities, and strengthening its presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul.
Founded in 2026 by Agarwal and Ishank Gupta, Humyn Labs has clocked an annualised revenue run rate of more than $50 million within six months of operations. The company works with frontier AI labs, robotics companies and world-model developers, collecting and processing data across more than 20 countries in Latin America, East Asia, and South and Southeast Asia.
Also Read
Unlike conventional AI systems, which primarily rely on digital datasets, physical AI models need to understand and interact with real-world environments. Humyn Labs captures how people perform tasks across factories, warehouses, farms and homes, and converts the information into training-ready data across sight, sound, motion and touch.
However, Agarwal said the company’s business goes beyond data collection. Its larger opportunity lies in helping robotics companies bridge the gap between model training and actual deployment. 
“Data collection is just the input side. The reason data is being collected is that you want robotic form factors to be deployed across different use cases. For deployment readiness, providing data is not enough. You need to start deploying these models and hardware in the real world,” he said.
The company plans to establish dedicated robot deployment centres, or what Agarwal described as “robot gyms,” where models and hardware can be tested in real-world settings. It also plans to work with large enterprises to establish such centres at their facilities globally.
While Humyn Labs is headquartered in Bengaluru, it has a subsidiary in the US, where around 95 per cent of its customer base is located. The company is prioritising San Francisco as its first international market, followed by London (UK) and Munich (Germany), with Seoul (South Korea) and Tokyo (Japan).
Despite being headquartered in India, Humyn Labs does not see the country as an immediate priority for commercial robot deployment. Agarwal said deployment readiness depends on two factors -- the cost economics of the robot and its ability to perform tasks reliably in real-world conditions. He added that India may take longer to become a priority market because the economics of deploying robots may not currently work across several use cases.

SEOUL, Nov 19 (Reuters) - South Korea's exports so far for this year have exceeded $1 trillion, driven by a global AI chip boom, making it the fourth country in the world to reach the milestone after Germany, the United States and China.
Exports passed the $1 trillion mark as of 0509 GMT on Thursday, compared with last year's record of $709 billion, the trade ministry said.
Asia's fourth-largest economy, home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, is riding the global boom in AI investment that is fuelling exports and investments.
Still, domestic demand remains weak with the benefits of the export boom yet to trickle down to many households. Consumer sentiment has been hurt by high interest rates and prices, as well as unprecedented volatility in the domestic stock market.
"Now, we need to turn this achievement into sustainable growth. We will enhance the competitiveness of major industries and grow future growth engines, such as AI and bio," President Lee Jae Myung said in a social media post on X.
"Most of all, the achievement in exports should improve the lives of the people. We will create 'growth for all', sharing the opportunities and fruits of growth with big and small companies as well as the capital area and regional areas," Lee said.
The Lee administration plans to create a 162.3 trillion won ($121.94 billion) Future Response Fund to funnel excess tax revenue from the chip boom toward growth industries, young people, regional development and education.
South Korea's economic growth is expected to quicken to the mid-3% range this year on record chip exports, after expanding 1% last year, the country's finance minister said last month.

AI surge could strain US capacity and overheat economy, Fed's Goolsbee says
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 : The booming rollout of artificial intelligence technology could strain the US economy's capacity and further boost inflation that the Federal Reserve will have to counteract, Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said on Thursday, as AI firm Anthropic set a new record for an initial public offering of stock.
"The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy. I find it hard to ... look at that any other way," Goolsbee said in a conference call with reporters. "When you're getting major business investment, almost unprecedented levels of business investment, there's a high danger that the economy's capacity cannot handle that kind of a pig through the python."
Goolsbee said he sees the multitrillion-dollar pipeline of data-center projects already adding to what he referred to as "borderline, disturbingly high inflation rates" that are well above the Fed's 2 per cent target and potentially heading higher.
He said he felt the Anthropic IPO, giving the company's early shareholders the ability to tap equity holdings well in excess of $1 trillion, could on its own become relevant to the path of the broader economy.
"A $1.5 trillion IPO. The question of what people are going to do with the money now that they have some access to that liquidity is going to become a macro-relevant statistic," Goolsbee said. "We're watching that."
DATA-CENTER BACKLASH
The US central bank is widely expected to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point at its December 8-9 meeting. Fed policymakers also are wrestling with how the AI boom is influencing the economy.
The recent US midterm elections saw AI skepticism emerge at the polls, with municipalities in a number of states approving ballot initiatives that could limit how quickly and where data centers get built, potentially slowing the industry's breakneck evolution.
At the same time, the Fed this week held a high-level conference looking at the possible impact on productivity and the labor market should the new technologies diffuse through the economy and reach a potential that Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has characterized as pivotal to US economic leadership.
In remarks at an earlier event on Thursday, Goolsbee said it was not yet clear what effect AI will have on productivity or the economy's underlying potential, noting that it took years — even decades — for other general-purpose technologies to change how businesses operated on a broad basis.
In the meantime, the Fed will have to cope with short-term effects that so far seem to be inflationary.
"The Fed's job is to prevent this thing from overheating the economy," with monetary policy set tight enough to keep demand and supply in balance, Goolsbee said at the event.
The Chicago Fed chief did not say if he would support a larger half-percentage-point rate hike at the December meeting, as at least one of his colleagues has advocated, but added that all options were on the table.
"The question of how steep the rate path is going to be and if there will be any rate increases should be determined, in my view, by whether you think inflation is going to be heading back to 2 per cent on its own or not," Goolsbee said. "The evidence does not suggest we're on a path back to 2 per cent."

work-careers-7b37e27002.headline: Karnataka hosts 51% of India’s GCCs and 43% of GCC AI/ML talent: Report
work-careers-7b37e27002.fulltext:
Updated - November 19, 2026  at 06:38 PM.
Karnataka is home to 1,088 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), accounting for 51 per cent of India’s total, and employs 111,000 AI and ML professionals, or 43 per cent of the country’s GCC AI/ML talent, according to a report by Zinnov in collaboration with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM).
The report, GCCs in Karnataka: Shaping the Future of Enterprise AI, found that more than 660 GCCs in the State have AI/ML capabilities and that over 120 dedicated AI/ML Centres of Excellence (CoEs) operate across more than 100 GCCs. Karnataka accounts for roughly 48 per cent of India’s AI/ML CoEs.
The State also hosts 320 GCCs belonging to Global 2000 companies, representing 63 per cent of such centres in India. Its installed GCC workforce exceeds 829,000, around 35 per cent of the national total, while its GCC engineering research and development workforce stands at more than 414,000, accounting for 41 per cent of India’s total.
“As artificial intelligence reshapes how global enterprises create value, Karnataka’s GCCs are playing an increasingly strategic role,” Priyank M Kharge, Minister for Home, IT and BT and e-Governance, Government of Karnataka, said.
The report said Karnataka attracted 217 of the 510 new GCCs established in India between FY2021 and FY2026E, accounting for 43 per cent of additions during the period. It also accounted for 46 of the 89 new GCCs set up by Global 2000 companies, and 90 of the 178 new Software and Internet GCCs.
Bengaluru continues to account for a significant share of demand for senior AI talent. The city represents 44 per cent of India’s AI leadership hiring demand, with demand 4.3 times that of the next city, according to the report. It also accounts for 63 per cent of the country’s demand for Distinguished and Principal AI Engineers, 55 per cent for AI Product Managers and 50 per cent for AI/ML Scientists. AI hiring intensity in Bengaluru rose from 8.5 per cent in 2024 to 13.6 per cent in 2026.
The report also found that Karnataka’s GCCs scored 1.12 times the national average on overall AI maturity. Around two-thirds of the surveyed GCCs in the State had reached the Portfolio Hub stage.
On AI adoption, 69 per cent of Karnataka GCCs had dedicated AI budgets, compared with 57 per cent nationally. The share of GCCs conducting role-specific AI training stood at 69 per cent, against 53 per cent across India. Further, 83 per cent of Karnataka GCCs reused in-house AI platforms across business units, compared with 57 per cent nationally.
However, only 42 per cent of the surveyed GCCs in Karnataka owned AI initiatives end-to-end, against 32 per cent nationally.
The State has more than 451,000 professionals in emerging technology roles—54 per cent of its GCC workforce. Its broader ecosystem includes over 29 per cent of India’s AI startups, 15.4 per cent of its incubators and accelerators, and more than 5,000 investors. Karnataka produces over 130,000 STEM graduates annually.
Kharge said the State was working to strengthen AI capabilities and research through its GCC Policy 2024-29 and IT Policy 2025-30.
“The Government of Karnataka remains steadfast in its commitment to enabling this growth. Through India’s first dedicated GCC Policy (2024-29) and our IT Policy 2025-30, we are strengthening AI capabilities, research and innovation across the state,” he said.
He added that Nipuna Karnataka was building future-ready skills through industry partnerships, while the Beyond Bengaluru initiative was extending opportunities to emerging cities. The State was also drafting a framework for ethical, safe and transparent AI in governance.
